A cancellation-safe clock for nilpotent bilinear
                         dynamics
                               Anonymous Authors


                                       Abstract
            We determine the exact time to zero for the bilinear map F (x, y) =
        (y, x(t + y)) on I 2 , where I = tFq [t]/(tm ), q is any prime power and
        m ≥ 2. With the truncated valuation normalized by v(0) = m, this
        time is max{2(m − v(y)), 2(m − v(x)) − 1}. The nonlinear term can
        cancel the leading term of one register, so a coordinatewise linear-clock
        argument does not suffice. After separating the two parity chains, the
        other register gives the sharp deadline even in the cancellation case.
        Consequently zero is the unique recurrent state, the maximum depth
        is 2m − 2, and exactly q h states have depth at most h for 0 ≤ h ≤
        2m − 2. We also evaluate every one-step fibre by an elementary ideal
        calculation. This inverse mechanism is multiplication under separate
        input and output translations, not a new inversion method. The clock
        and depth distribution agree with a linear control, but for m ≥ 3
        unequal nonempty fibre sizes exclude conjugacy to any finite-group
        endomorphism. The case m = 2 is precisely the linear boundary.


1      The map and the question
Nilpotence forces many finite algebraic systems to lose information, but it
does not determine when both registers of a coupled recurrence vanish. For
the map studied here, a leading-term cancellation can erase one register ear-
lier than a linear model predicts. The exact full-state deadline nevertheless
agrees with that model. Our purpose is to prove this agreement on the
full carrier, including the cancellation locus, and to distinguish it from a
linearization of the dynamics.
    Throughout, q is a prime power, m ≥ 2, and

    R = Fq [t]/(tm ),     I = tR,       F : I 2 −→ I 2 ,   F (x, y) = (y, x(t + y)).
                                                                                 (1.1)



                                           1
 The symbol t denotes its residue class in R. For a nonzero element z, let v(z)
be the least degree of its nonzero coefficients, and put v(0) = m. Coefficient
multiplication and counting give
    v(zw) = min{m, v(z) + v(w)},            |tr R| = q m−r   (0 ≤ r ≤ m).   (1.2)
An element with nonzero constant coefficient is a unit: factoring out that
coefficient reduces its inverse to a finite geometric series. In particular,
v(t + z) = 1 whenever z ∈ t2 R.
    For s ∈ I 2 , define its depth by τ (s) = min{n ∈ Z≥0 : F n (s) = (0, 0)},
initially allowing infinity. A state is recurrent if some positive iterate returns
to it. We prove that all depths are finite and that
               τ (x, y) = max{2(m − v(y)), 2(m − v(x)) − 1}.                (1.3)
The associated depth count and the full target-fibre count follow from dif-
ferent calculations: the first uses parity chains, the second uses the image
and kernel of multiplication on I.
     Endomorphism dynamics provide a useful comparison class: their finite
state graphs have structural restrictions coming from the group operation
[1]. The present map is not assumed to be an endomorphism. Multiplicative
feedback also occurs in the complex Fibonacci maps (x, y) 7→ (xy + c, x) [2].
At c = 0, interchanging coordinates gives the polynomial (x, y) 7→ (y, xy).
This is background for the one-step multiplication relation, not a transfer
of complex dynamics to the nilpotent ideal in (1.1).
     The contribution is the cancellation-safe temporal theorem for this ex-
plicit nonlinear map. Neither the resulting numerical clock shape nor the
general valuation-contraction method is asserted to be new. We evaluate
the one-step inverse completely while explicitly deducting its multiplication
mechanism in Section 4. Equal depth distributions will not be confused with
conjugate state graphs.


2    The exact clock
The recurrence representation isolates the only multiplier at which leading-
term cancellation matters.
Lemma 2.1. Set x0 = x, x1 = y and
                        xn+2 = xn (t + xn+1 )     (n ≥ 0).                  (2.1)
Then F n (x, y) = (xn , xn+1 ). Every xn belongs to I, and xn ∈ t2 R for n ≥ 2.
Thus v(t + xn ) = 1 for n ≥ 2.

                                        2
 Proof. The iterate identity follows by induction from (1.1). If two consecu-
tive terms belong to I, both factors on the right of (2.1) belong to I, so their
product belongs to t2 R ⊆ I. Starting with x, y ∈ I proves both inclusions.
The last claim follows from the coefficient of t in t + xn .

Theorem 2.2 (Pointwise clock). For every (x, y) ∈ I 2 , formula (1.3) holds.
Zero is the unique recurrent state. The maximum depth is 2m − 2, attained
exactly at the states with v(y) = 1.

Proof. Write a = v(x) and b = v(y). First suppose b ≥ 2. The initial multi-
plier t + y and every later multiplier in (2.1) have valuation one. Induction
therefore gives, for k ≥ 0,

          v(x2k ) = min{m, a + k},           v(x2k+1 ) = min{m, b + k}.      (2.2)

If a < m, the last nonzero even-indexed term has index 2(m−a−1); if b < m,
the last nonzero odd-indexed term has index 2(m − b − 1) + 1. The first
zero state occurs one index after the last nonzero term, giving the maximum
in (1.3). If a = m, the even chain is absent and its displayed contribution
is −1, which cannot dominate the nonnegative odd-chain contribution. If
b = m, the odd chain is absent and contributes zero. In particular a = b = m
gives depth zero.
    Now suppose b = 1. Cancellation in t + y can only accelerate the even
chain. Lemma 2.1 and (1.2) imply

v(x2k ) ≥ min{m, a + k} (k ≥ 1),             v(x2k+1 ) = min{m, 1 + k}(k ≥ 0).
                                                                           (2.3)
For the second equality, the first update of the odd chain uses t+x2 ; all such
adjacent even terms lie in t2 R. Hence x2m−3 ̸= 0 but x2m−2 = x2m−1 = 0,
proving τ = 2m − 2. Since a ≥ 1, this is exactly (1.3). The argument
includes m = 2.
    Every state reaches the fixed state zero, so no other state is recurrent.
When b ≥ 2, both contributions to (1.3) are at most 2m − 3; when b = 1,
the depth is 2m − 2. This proves sharpness and its equality condition.

   For example, (t, −t) has x2 = 0, whereas for k ≥ 1 its iterates are

           F 2k (t, −t) = (0, −tk+1 ),       F 2k+1 (t, −t) = (−tk+1 , 0).   (2.4)

Powers are taken modulo tm . The first zero state is still 2m − 2; an exact
valuation increment for both chains would have been false.


                                         3
 Corollary 2.3 (Depth census). For every integer 0 ≤ h ≤ 2m − 2, exactly
q h states have depth at most h. Depth zero has one state, and each depth
1 ≤ h ≤ 2m − 2 has (q − 1)q h−1 states.

Proof. The two inequalities in (1.3) give

        τ (x, y) ≤ h   ⇐⇒     v(x) ≥ m − ⌈h/2⌉,     v(y) ≥ m − ⌊h/2⌋.

Both thresholds lie between 1 and m. Formula (1.2) therefore gives q ⌈h/2⌉ q ⌊h/2⌋ =
q h states. Subtract the count at h−1 for the exact positive-depth count.


3    Complete one-step fibres
The inverse fixes one register and leaves a multiplication equation in I.
The final valuation stratum requires the kernel inside I, rather than the
annihilator in all of R.

Theorem 3.1 (Target fibres). Fix (u, w) ∈ I 2 and set d = min{v(t+u), m−
1}. The target is reachable if and only if w ∈ td+1 R. If it is reachable and
x0 is one solution of (t + u)x0 = w in I, its full predecessor set is

                 F −1 ({(u, w)}) = {(x0 + k, u) : k ∈ tm−d R},            (3.1)

and has cardinality q d .

Proof. The first target coordinate forces y = u, so the remaining equation
is (t + u)x = w with x ∈ I. If d ≤ m − 2, write t + u = td e for a unit e.
Multiplication by e permutes every ideal tr R. Consequently multiplication
by t + u maps I onto td+1 R and has kernel tm−d R. For w = td+1 w0 , a
concrete solution is x0 = te−1 w0 ; choosing another lift of w0 changes this
solution only by the kernel. Two solutions differ by a kernel element, and
adding any kernel element preserves the equation. This proves (3.1) in this
case.
    If d = m − 1, then t + u ∈ tm−1 R and (t + u)I = 0, including the case
t + u = 0. The only reachable second coordinate is w = 0, and every x ∈ I
is then a solution. Here td+1 R = 0 and tm−d R = I, so the same formula
applies. The ideal cardinality in (1.2) gives q d .

Corollary 3.2 (Distribution and extreme fibres). For 1 ≤ d ≤ m − 2,
exactly
                           (q − 1)q 2(m−d−1)                   (3.2)


                                       4
 targets have q d predecessors. Exactly q targets have the largest fibre size
q m−1 ; they are
                        (−t + ctm−1 , 0),   c ∈ Fq .                   (3.3)
The image size is
                                                   m−2
                                                   X
                          | im F | = q + (q − 1)         q 2j .                  (3.4)
                                                   j=1

All remaining targets have empty fibres. An empty sum is zero.

Proof. Translation u 7→ t + u permutes I. For each ordinary stratum 1 ≤
d ≤ m − 2, exactly (q − 1)q m−d−1 values of u give valuation d. For each
such u, there are q m−d−1 admissible values of w. Their product is (3.2).
The saturated condition t + u ∈ tm−1 R instead has the q solutions in (3.3),
each permitting only w = 0. These fibres are larger than all ordinary ones.
Summing their counts gives (3.4). At m = 2 there is no ordinary stratum:
all q reachable targets have q predecessors.


4    Multiplication and linear controls
The fibre theorem is an evaluated multiplication relation. On the same
carrier I 2 , define

    M (a, b) = (b, ab),      P (x, y) = (x, y + t),          Q(u, w) = (u − t, w).

Both P and Q are bijections, and direct substitution gives

                                  F = Q ◦ M ◦ P.                                 (4.1)

Thus every one-step fibre and image count transfers from multiplication. No
new inverse mechanism is claimed. Since Q ̸= P −1 , this two-sided identity
is not an iterate conjugacy and does not supply the temporal proof.

The two inequalities in~\eqref{eq:preview} give

 \tau(x,y)\leq h\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 v(x)\geq m-\lceil h/2\rceil,\quad

Both thresholds lie between $1$ and $m$. Formula~\eqref{eq:ideals}
therefore gives $q^{\lceil h/2\rceil}q^{\lfloor h/2\rfloor}=q^h$
states. Subtract the count at $h-1$ for the exact positive-depth count.

\section{Verification scope and limitations}
\label{sec:scope}

The proofs above hold for every prime power $q$ and every $m\geq2$.
The accompanying author-verifier source is restricted to
$q\in\{2,3,4\}$ and $m\in\{2,3,4\}$. It is designed to enumerate every
state, its literal transition and orbit-derived depth, and the full
predecessor set of every target, before checking the displayed formulas.
For $q=4$ the coefficient field is
$\mathbb F_2[\alpha]/(\alpha^2+\alpha+1)$, not arithmetic modulo four.
At this source-draft stage, no execution or computational result is claimed.

The result is specific to~\eqref{eq:map} on the full ideal square $I^2$.
It establishes neither an arbitrary-chain-ring extension nor all-time fibre
formulas or a classification of functional-graph isomorphisms. The temporal
conclusion is narrower: leading-term cancellation changes one register's
history without changing the exact deadline of the full nonlinear state.
